prize_parts.citation: for pioneering large-volume neutrino telescopes and the observation of a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, opening neutrino astronomy

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single prize for IceCube, to Halzen and Spiering. After the full exchange I still think the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux is the one result on this shortlist that is a new clue from nature in the strict sense: a messenger at TeV-PeV energies, measured in several independent channels over more than a decade, whose existence is no longer in dispute and whose origin is a question that has now become a field. The citation can and should rest on that flux and on the telescopes that made it measurable, and not on TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068 or the Galactic plane at 3-4 sigma. That is the same discipline I would ask of any citation here. The chair is right that the committee must ask what is gained by waiting; for IceCube the answer is that the discovery is already secure and the interpretive uncertainty is exactly the part the citation need not claim. I do take seriously that B042 is the most broadly supported and the most mature configuration, and I have moved it to first alternative, but breadth of ranking is not the same as strength of the discovery case, and I do not want to follow a count.
statement.case_against: Support for B032 in round 1 is a single explicit vote, mine, with Pearce listing it as his first alternative, so I may be misjudging how the committee will read it. Individual sources remain below 5 sigma, and the field may look different in five years. The credit is the real weak point: AMANDA, Baikal, DUMAND and ANTARES pioneers are not covered, and I have not seen anything in this exchange that settles whether Spiering's role is as decisive as Halzen's. If the expert evaluations I would normally commission say Spiering is not clearly one of the two or three people without whom the telescopes would not exist, the pairing falls and I would not want to defend it. A two-name award for a collaboration of hundreds will also be criticised as selective whichever names are chosen.

responses.point: Argues that B042 rests on a concrete idea (magic-wavelength trapping), has been reproduced at 1e-18 across JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB and NIST, produces new science (millimetre redshift, constants, dark matter), and has the cleanest two-name attribution; asks why wait when the case is complete.
responses.response: I accept the maturity and the independent reproduction, and I accept that Katori and Ye is a tidier pair than anything else except possibly mine. My disagreement is about what kind of result it is. Millimetre redshift and limits on dark-matter couplings are things the clocks make possible; they are not yet things the clocks have found. A third prize on the frequency-standards line after 2005 and 2012 therefore asks the committee to value an improvement in a measurement over a new window on nature, and I would put the window first. I do not think your case is weak, and your point that waiting buys nothing for B042 is fair. But the same argument applies to B032, whose central discovery is also complete. If the committee decides it wants the metrology line, I can vote B042 and would not call it a mistake, provided the citation names the lattice clock and not the redefinition of the second, which is a decision and not a discovery.

responses.point: Moved to B042 first on breadth of ranking (seven of eight members) and instrument maturity, while keeping B032 as the first alternative and noting that B032 is a more direct new observational window but has support from only three members and sub-5-sigma sources.
responses.response: Thank you for the candour: you are the other person who knows this field well, and you moved on the evidence of support rather than on the science. I would resist that move. Counting how many colleagues ranked a candidate in an opening ballot told us where tastes overlapped, but the round-1 exchange has shown that most of that overlap for B042 is lukewarm, with fourth to seventh places from Olsson, Eriksson and Mehlig. Your own reservation about sources at 3-4 sigma is the one I would answer directly: that is why I want the citation on the flux and the telescopes. On the 2002 prize, which you raised in your opening, I still see no obstacle; Davis and Koshiba observed MeV solar and supernova neutrinos, and a PeV extragalactic flux is a different thing. Your open question about whether the early AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND leaders are slighted is the one thing I would want settled before the vote, and I would ask the Secretary's office, which is me, to put it to outside experts.

responses.point: Prefers B019 (Bistritzer-MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero) as theory anticipating a new quantum state with broad reproduction, while saying B042 is the better-settled discovery if the committee judges the field too young.
responses.response: I still admire the prediction followed by observation, and I said in round 1 that I would not oppose B019 this year. What has moved me, reading your statement and the others, is how often the omission of Yuan Cao and the earlier Lopes dos Santos twist-angle theory comes up as something the citation must manage, and that the pairing mechanism for the superconductivity is still contested. A citation limited to the flat bands and the observed phases is honest, but it is a narrower prize than the public will read it as, and the mechanism could change the picture within a few years. You say yourself that B042 is the better-settled discovery. For a committee that wants a condensed-matter prize I could support B019 as second alternative, but I would still ask whether we are rewarding a very active field at the moment it is most interesting, not the moment it is most settled.

responses.point: Judges B042 the candidate she can check most directly and the most cleanly attributed, flags that her own atomic-physics taste may overvalue precision, and asks whether the committee counts clocks as a discovery about nature or a metrology instrument.
responses.response: That last question is exactly the one I think decides between us, and I appreciate you stating your own bias, since I am doing the same: I favour the observational discovery because I am a theorist who distrusts elegance without clues. I read the will as permitting an invention or a discovery, so I do not think B042 is excluded, and your checking of the systematics is exactly the evidence I would want. Where we differ is that I think the 2005 and 2012 prizes make the marginal metrology award less compelling than the first neutrinos beyond the solar and supernova regime. If a majority of the committee reads the clocks as opening a new regime for tests of fundamental physics, I will not stand in the way, but I would want the citation to name that regime and not just the 10^-18 number.

responses.point: Moved to B042 after reading the openings, arguing that it has the broadest support and reproducibility, but worries a prize may be better after the redefinition of the second and notes that B019 has the mechanism question still open.
responses.response: We agree that B019 should wait for the pairing mechanism to clarify, and that is a more solid reason for waiting than the age of the field alone. Your concern that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened cuts the other way from how it is usually used: I do not think B042 should wait for it, since a redefinition is a decision about units and not a scientific result. Where I disagree is on weight: a majority of rankings in an opening ballot is not evidence of a stronger discovery, as your own admission about B049 shows when you say that familiarity can bias a first place. I would apply the same caution to the clock cluster as a whole.

uncertainties: Whether Spiering's role is as decisive as Halzen's relative to the other early large-volume telescope leaders; this is the point on which my configuration could fail and I would want the outside evaluations to answer it directly.

Whether the committee will accept a citation on the diffuse flux and the telescopes alone while individual sources remain at 3-4 sigma, or will want to wait for source identification at higher significance.
Whether the lack of support for B032 in round 1 reflects a scientific judgement I have not understood or merely the order of opening rankings; I cannot tell from the statements.
Whether the committee is willing to place a new observational window above the metrology line after the 2005 and 2012 prizes, which is the central disagreement with the B042 supporters.
statement.conflict_note: No apparent conflict with any shortlisted candidate: my connections are Gross, Rubinstein (deceased), Van Riet and the Uppsala string-theory group, none credited on any ballot. As Secretary I commission outside evaluations and will keep that role separate from advocacy; I note that I am proposing a question to the experts on B032 whose answer could change my own position.
